claims.text: Decreasing the size of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles lowers their effective thermal stability.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles undergo structural or phase transitions at lower temperatures than larger particles.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Atomistic molecular-dynamics simulations can be used to examine the temperature-dependent behavior of HEA nanostructures.
Replica exchange molecular dynamics is an appropriate method for studying the size-dependent thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
The proposed simulations compare nanoparticle diameters from below 10 nm to larger sizes under progressive heating, comparable composition, and vacuum conditions.
Decreasing nanoparticle size increases the surface-to-volume ratio.
The greater surface-to-volume ratio of smaller nanoparticles enhances surface effects.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have higher defect densities.
Enhanced sampling by REMD captures the relevant free-energy landscape.
Surface-driven effects in smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles reduce the energy barriers for phase transitions and structural rearrangements.
Heating can produce structural, chemical, phase, or morphological changes in multicomponent alloy nanostructures.
Larger nanoparticles or bulk HEA systems generally have greater thermal stability and require higher temperatures for transitions comparable to those in smaller nanoparticles.
The proposed size dependence is limited to FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles under the specified simulated heating conditions and may differ in other environments or compositions.
The precise transition temperatures and energy-barrier differences are uncertain.
Radial distribution functions and coordination numbers can be used as structural indicators of phase changes in the proposed simulations.
